tool.excerpt: On 3 September 2026, the Houthis launched an offensive against the Saudi-backed and UN recognized Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), the internationally recognized government of Yemen, amid the ongoing Yemeni civil war. Clashes began in Taiz Governorate, prompting a PLC counter-offensive against the Houthis in the Al-Jawf and Al-Bayda governorates. The fighting coincides with the ongoing 2026 Iran war, which has marked the deadliest fighting in Yemen since the collapse of the 2022 ceasefire. The Yemeni government lost areas around the Bab al-Mandab Strait in Yemen's southwest after a swift battle over Mokha, resulting in a crisis with the entire west coast of Yemen (except for the Midi district) falling under control of the Houthi movement, who named the operation as Operation Allah is Stronger in Might and More Severe in Punishment. The counteroffensive of the PLC against the Houthis was named Operation Dawn of Yemen. == Background == === 2022 ceasefire and the Red Sea crisis === The Houthis and the internationally recognized government of Yemen reached a ceasefire agreement in 2022, which largely held until the 2026 campaign. Peace talks stalled in 2023 amidst the Gaza war. Starting on 19 October 2023, the Houthis began launching missiles and drones at international shipping crossing the Bab al-Mandab Strait in solidarity with Palestinians during the war in Gaza, triggering the Red Sea crisis. In response, a US-led multinational coalition launched Operation Prosperity Guardian in late 2023 to secure shipping through the Red Sea. In early 2024, the United States and the United Kingdom launched a series of airstrikes targeting Houthi missile and drone launch sites across Yemen. In March 2025, the United States launched a larger wave of strikes against the Houthis, after which the Houthis agreed to stop attacking U.S. vessels in the Red Sea. Additionally, Israel previously launched a series of airstrikes on Houthi-controlled Yemen in response to missile attacks by the group, including a July 2024 strike on Tel Aviv that killed one person. sentences: Yemen’s Houthis attacked Aden’s international airport with ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones earlier on Wednesday, the country’s transport ministry said.
Credit: AAP Three people have been killed in attacks on Saudi airports, as fighting intensified in Yemen between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces.
Aden International Airport is the main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside Houthi control.

This week, Yemeni government forces with Saudi-led coalition air support launched a counter-offensive to recapture strategic territory near the strait and around the town of Mocha that the Houthi rebels had captured in September but it is unclear if their advance will hold.
Houthi fighters, who control much of Yemen’s north, seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a military coalition led by Saudi Arabia to intervene.
Staff Writers Reuters 2 Min Read 08 Oct 2026 Updated 08 Oct 2026 Yemeni government forces say they have made advances against Houthi rebels.

The country’s civil aviation authorities said one person was killed and eight wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, and two were killed and 28 wounded in an attack on facilities at Abha airport.
The Saudi airport attacks were among a series of strikes targeting aviation infrastructure.
One missile landed near the runway at Aden International Airport minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land, according to officials.
The fighting has revived a complex 12-year war in Yemen that led to one of the worst humanitarian crises globally and fragmented the Arab world’s most impoverished country.
The United Nations says three in four families are going hungry in parts of Yemen.

Any Houthi stranglehold on the strait could threaten shipping or global oil flows, and Saudi Arabia has been seeking international assistance to repel the Houthi movement.

Hussam Radman, a researcher at the Sanaa Center, a Yemen-focused think tank, said pro-government forces including the Giants Brigade, a conservative Sunni Salafi group that has led the counter-offensive, are trying to take control of Dhubab and to advance in the mountains to its east.

It also shares maritime borders with Djibouti, Eritrea, and Somalia across the Horn of Africa.
